The model uses a 27 x 18 x 7 element grid in the x, r, and θ directions to represent the combustor geometry.
The air flow was divided such that 7.8% entered through the swirler, 25.5% through the primary jets, 29.9% through the secondary jets, and 36.8% through the dilution jets.
The Rosin-Rammler parameters used to represent the fuel spray were D = 60 μm and n = 2.2, based on experimental measurements.
The total air flow rate was 2.125 x 10^-2 kg/s, the fuel flow rate was 6.92 x 10^-4 kg/s, and the air inlet temperature was 351 K.
The swirl number of the inlet air flow was 0.8, and the initial droplet velocity was -20 m/s.
The model was able to accurately predict the high temperature region following the hollow spray cone, as well as the cooler core caused by the major recirculation eddy.
A large number of droplets were found to hit the combustor walls, although the majority of the fuel was evaporated near the spray.
The presence of combustion significantly enhanced the recirculation vortex and increased the overall velocity magnitudes compared to the cold, droplet-free case.
The exit temperature profile exhibited a minimum on the axis and a maximum near the walls, consistent with experimental observations.
The authors note that the generality of the computational procedure allows it to be applied to other gas-particle flow problems beyond gas turbine combustors.
